  host password inside it, so a guessable one lets anybody start a meeting as
  host. If yours looks weak the server logs one warning and **meeting links keep
  working** - nothing stops, but it is worth rotating. `docs/guides/calendar.md`
  explains how.

  Finally, a tooling fix that matters more than it sounds: findings the code
  scanner had already been told to ignore were being filed as security alerts
  nobody could ever close. A real new finding would have arrived in that list
  looking exactly like the known-harmless ones. Those are no longer published, so
  the list means something again.
- **A security advisory in a Prisma dependency stopped the test suite from
  running, and is now closed (#2945).** A high-severity advisory published on
  17 August affected a package Prisma depends on. The dependency audit runs
  early in CI and skips everything after it when it fails, so for a period the
  unit tests and the build were not running on any branch even though other
  checks reported green. The affected package is pinned to a fixed version,
  which required no change to Prisma itself, and a check now reports when the
  pin can be removed again.
- **One-time link tokens no longer sit in a page's links or attributes (#2827).**
  Site-Style **Raw CSS** is a trusted admin capability, but a CSS attribute
  selector can read a value one character at a time - so on the pages that carry
  Raw CSS, any secret in an attribute was readable by whoever edits the club's
  styling, which includes a content-area admin who is not a Full Admin. Two
  places were putting a one-time token where it did not belong, and both are
  closed.

  On the group-join confirmation page, the "if you are not redirected" fallback
  was a link containing the pay-by-link token, on a page that **does** carry Raw
  CSS. It is now a button that navigates from the token the page already holds in
  memory, so nothing selectable carries it. The automatic redirect is unchanged,
  and no path is lost - reaching that screen at all requires the Confirm step that
  fetches the token.

  The footer's per-page styling hook (`data-page-slug`, which lets Raw CSS target
  one page) was stamping the raw address on the one-time-link pages under the
  login area, so it carried the token itself on `/pay`, `/chores`,
  `/family-invite` and `/membership-cancellation`. It now stamps the route shape -
  `pay/[token]` - exactly as the rest of the site already did, so styling one page
  still works and the token is gone. Those particular pages do not inject Raw CSS,
  so this is precaution rather than a hole being closed; it means the day they are
  moved under the shared page chrome, they cannot start leaking silently. A new
  one-time-link page added there without being registered now fails a test. The
  same work fixed a styling bug it uncovered: the membership application form
  (`/join/apply`) was being labelled as the group-join code page, so a club's CSS
  rule for either one landed on the wrong page.

  Nothing an operator has to configure, and no page a member sees looks different.
- **Setting up a local backup directory no longer requires knowing how Docker
  works (#2977).** Two things went wrong for the first operator who tried
  it, and both are fixed.

  On a containerised deployment - which the shipped Docker Compose stack is -
  the backup directory is the path **inside the container**, not on the server,
  because that container has a read-only filesystem and can only write to a
  directory mounted into it. Entering a host path such as
  `/home/alpineclub/db_backup` failed with `Could not create that directory:
  ENOENT` - accurate and useless. The message now says so when the application
  really is containerised, names the mounted path when there is one, and
  otherwise gives the two steps needed to create it, including the ownership
  change most people would hit next. Running the application directly on a
  server? Nothing here changes for you.

  The directory is also configurable per deployment now, so each club can put it
  where their server has room. Set `BACKUP_LOCAL_HOST_DIR` in `.env` to a host
  directory and `docker compose up -d app`; it is bind-mounted at
  `BACKUP_LOCAL_DIR` (`/backups` by default), and the Backups page **fills that
  path in for you** - nothing to retype and nothing to mistype. Leave
  `BACKUP_LOCAL_HOST_DIR` empty and backups go to a named volume instead, which
  needs no setup at all but keeps the files inside Docker. A path saved on the
  Backups page still overrides both.

  Existing installations are unaffected: the default is the named volume, and no
  backup starts writing anywhere until an admin enables local backups.
- **The Node heap for `docker compose build` can now be set from `.env`
  (#2977).** On a server with limited memory, `next build` - the memory peak
  of the whole image build - can be killed part-way, sometimes with nothing
  more informative than "JavaScript heap out of memory". The only remedy was
  editing the `Dockerfile` by hand, which then had to be removed before every
  `git pull` and re-applied afterwards.

  Set `NODE_BUILD_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096` in `.env` instead. It
  reaches `next build` as `NODE_OPTIONS` inside the builder stage and nothing
  else - not the running container, not your shell. Empty by default, so every
  existing deployment builds exactly as it did before.

  If your server is tight on memory, the better answer is not to build there at
  all: point `APP_IMAGE` at an image CI has already published and
  `docker compose up -d` pulls it rather than compiling.
- **The kiosk PIN a hut leader types can no longer be read by the club's own
  Site Appearance styling (#2981).** The club can add its own CSS to the public
  website from Admin > Site Appearance, and the page where a hut leader enters
  their six-digit kiosk PIN is one of the pages that styling reaches. Because of
  the way the page was built, the browser was publishing each character of the
  PIN as it was typed, in a form that a stylesheet could read one character at a
  time - so anyone who could edit the club's styling could have recovered a hut
  leader's PIN without ever seeing the screen.

  This was checked in three real browsers before anything was changed, because
  the original evidence came from a simulated browser and a simulation is not
  proof about the real thing. Chrome, Firefox and Safari all behaved the same
  way, and all three published the PIN. They no longer do: the PIN field now
  holds what is typed in a place a stylesheet cannot reach at all, and a browser
  test types a known PIN character by character and fails if a single character
  ever becomes readable again.

  Nothing changes for a hut leader: the field looks the same, accepts only six
  digits as before, and its password-manager behaviour is unchanged. Nothing
  changes for an administrator either - the club's Raw CSS feature is untouched
  and still does everything it did before.
- **The family-group invitation link no longer leaves the invite code in your
  browser's address bar or history.** The "I already have an account" and "Sign
  in with a different account" buttons on an invitation used to carry the
  invitation's own code in their web address, so it appeared in the address bar
  and stayed in the browser's history afterwards - where a shared or family
  computer keeps it, and where anything that records addresses can pick it up.

  The sign-in button is now an ordinary link, and where to send you afterwards is
  remembered privately by the server instead: in a short-lived cookie the page
  itself cannot read, written only when somebody actually opens the invitation,
  discarded the moment the sign-in lands back on it, and expiring after two
  minutes in any case.

  Nothing changes for the person invited. The emailed link still works, signing
  in still brings them back to the invitation, the sign-in button still works
  with JavaScript switched off, and if the remembered address has expired they
  simply land on their usual page instead.

  If you are signed in as a different member, that page now offers **"Sign out
  and use a different account"**, which actually works - the old button sent you
  straight back to the same screen.

  Nothing an operator has to configure.
- **On a shared computer, opening somebody's invitation no longer shows it to the
  next person who signs in.** Remembering the invitation privately on the server
  fixed the address-bar problem above, but it remembered it for the whole
  *browser* rather than for the one tab. So if a member opened an invitation on a
  lodge or club computer, changed their mind and walked off without signing in,
  the next person to sign in on that computer within the next two minutes was
  taken to that invitation - where they could read who it was sent to and which
  family group it was for. They could never actually join it (the page still
  checks that the signed-in member's email matches the one invited), but they
  should not have seen it at all.

  The invitation is now tied to the tab it was opened in. Sign in from that tab
  and you are brought back to the invitation exactly as before, whichever way you
  sign in - password, Google, or through a two-factor challenge. Sign in from
  anywhere else and you land on your usual page, with nothing about somebody
  else's invitation on the screen.

  **One deliberate change for the invited person.** If you ask for a sign-in link
  by email rather than typing your password, that emailed link opens in a fresh
  tab, so it is no longer treated as coming from the invitation. You will land on
  your usual page after signing in; open the invitation link again from your email
  and it will let you join, which is what the page already asks you to do. Every
  other way of signing in still takes you straight back to the invitation.

  Nothing an operator has to configure.
- **This site now knows whether it is the club's live site or a copy of it, and
  it never guesses (#3034).** A copy restored from the live database holds the
  club's real members and their real email addresses, so anything that leaves the
  app - a booking confirmation, a reminder, an invoice into the club's Xero
  organisation - needs to know which installation it is running on first.

  Each deployment now states it outright, in one setting on the server:
  `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE=production` for the club's live site, or
  `non-production` for a staging site, a rehearsal copy or a developer's
  machine. Nothing is inferred from the hostname, the branch, the database it is
  pointed at, or the `NODE_ENV` build mode - every one of those looks identical
  on a copy of the live site, which is exactly the case that matters.

  Where nothing has said, the answer is **"not configured"** rather than either
  one, and that is deliberate: it is not treated as the live site, and it is not
  treated as a copy either. A new **Production Or Non-Production** step on the
  setup checklist reports it, and start-up logs it.

  A Full Administrator can also force any installation to be treated as a copy,
  at **Admin → Setup & Configuration → Environment Safety**. That switch can only
  ever make the answer safer - there is no setting anywhere in the app that can
  declare an installation to be the live site, which is what stops a restored
  copy of the live database from claiming to be one. Turning it off hands the
  decision back to the deployment's own setting rather than promoting the copy.
  Both directions are Full-Administrator-only, need an explicit confirmation, and
  are recorded in the audit log with who did it and the value before and after.

  **Existing live deployments must add `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE=production` before
  upgrading.** The production deploy script refuses to run without it, at step 3
  of 20 - before the database migration and long before any traffic moves - so an
  undeclared upgrade stops with the previous release still serving and nothing
  changed, rather than succeeding and quietly holding back member email.

  It refuses the opposite mistake too, and that one is easier to make: the deploy
  script deploys the club's live site and nothing else, so it also refuses a
  `.env` that says `non-production`. The sample file ships `non-production`
  because it is a local-development template, and it is also the file people diff
  against their real settings when upgrading - so copying that value across would
  otherwise have produced a live site quietly behaving as a copy. Watch out for
  the near-miss as well: this is `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE`, not the
  `APP_RUNTIME_ROLE` already beside it, which names the container slot and is
  never read for this. After the deploy, check the **Production Or
  Non-Production** step on Admin → Setup actually reads *production*: a
  non-production installation shows a green tick too, so it is the message that
  carries the answer, not the tick.
  `docs/guides/environment-role.md` is the full walkthrough, and
  `docs/UPGRADING.md` has the upgrade step.

  **One more audit entry is readable at support level.** Switching the safer
  override on or off records an `ENVIRONMENT_SAFETY_OVERRIDE_UPDATED` entry filed
  under the **admin** category, which admins holding support access can read
  without membership access. The entry holds the value of that one switch before
  and after, and who changed it - no member details, no settings values and
  nothing about the database. It is filed as admin rather than security because it
  records a change to what this installation *does*, not to who may sign in or
  what they may reach.

  **The deploy also asks each container what it actually received.** Validating
  the settings file and validating what the containers were given turn out to be
  different questions: Docker Compose prefers a value set in the shell the deploy
  was started from over the one in the file, and reads the last of any duplicate
  assignments rather than the first. So the deploy now refuses a duplicated entry -
  in any of the shapes a settings file normally carries, including an indented
  or `export `-prefixed line - and refuses a shell value that disagrees with the
  file. Then, with the new release started and the previous one still serving
  every request, it asks each container which answer the application itself read,
  stopping before the switch-over if any of them says anything other than
  production. It asks the app rather than re-reading the container's settings so
  there is only ever one implementation of the rule.

  **Fewer deploys refused for no good reason.** An `export ` prefix, spaces around
  the `=`, or quotes round the value used to abort the deploy - the first two
  reported as a missing entry for a setting plainly present in the file. All three
  are now read the way Docker Compose reads them.

  **A copy says so in its own start-up log.** An installation that comes up as a
  copy now records one line saying so, and which of the two sources decided it, so
  somebody reading the log of a site brought up by hand can tell that a live club
  has been declared a copy by mistake. Alongside it, the Environment Safety page
  and the setup checklist have a place for how much application email has been
  held back - shown whenever delivery is being held back, whether the installation
  is a declared copy or has not been declared at all. That number is what tells a
  busy live club apart from an idle test copy. Nothing counts it yet, and the page
  says so in those words rather than showing a zero, because "none held back" and
  "not counted yet" mean opposite things. The counting arrives with #3035.

  This release records and reports the answer; the parts that act on it - holding
  back email to members, and keeping a copy's invoices out of the club's real
  accounting - follow in #3035 and #3036, so do not yet treat a copy as safe to
  run against real member data.
- Setting up a lodge kiosk login now needs a Full Admin. Opening the kiosk page
  still shows what is there to anyone who can view lodge settings, but the first
  kiosk account is only created when a Full Admin opens it - previously any
  officer who could view the page brought the account into existence just by
  loading it, including the read-only admin role, which is described to clubs as
  being able to view without making changes. Nothing changes for a club that
  already has a kiosk, and a Full Admin setting one up sees no extra step.
- **A hut leader's PIN no longer leaves the shared lodge tablet privileged all
  day.** Typing the kiosk PIN used to unlock the wall screen for **twelve
  hours**, with nothing anywhere that could end it early - so a tablet PINned in
  after breakfast was still a hut leader's screen at ten that night, to whoever
  walked up to it. The unlock now lasts **10 minutes of nobody touching the
  screen**, and there is a **Lock hut leader controls** button for walking away
  sooner. Continuous use keeps it unlocked, so somebody marking off a full lodge
  is never dropped part-way through - and that includes the **chore-roster
  wizard**, which is a separate screen: touching either page keeps the unlock
  alive, so a long roster setup reaches Confirm with everything intact. If the
  screen does lock itself mid-wizard, nothing is lost: the allocation stays
  exactly as it was and the PIN box appears at the top of the page, with the
  interrupted step re-running itself once the PIN goes in.

  The tablet refreshing itself in the background deliberately does **not** count
  as use, which is what stops an unattended device holding its own session open.
  The deadline lives inside the signed session cookie and is set by the server,
  and renewal exists in exactly one endpoint - a source census fails any other
  module that writes, names or extends that cookie. Behind the idle window sits
  an unchanged **12-hour ceiling** from the moment the PIN was typed, which no
  amount of use moves; it is the bound on the two cases the idle window cannot
  help with, and both are written up for operators: a tablet running anti-sleep
  software that taps its own screen, and an unlock copied off the device.
  Changing a hut leader's PIN still ends every unlock made with the old one at
  once.

  On a lock or a timeout the kiosk drops every privileged answer it is holding
  and asks again, so nothing a hut leader could see is left on screen or in the
  page's data even when the network is down at that moment; if the lock itself
  fails, a banner stays beside the button saying the screen is still unlocked
  rather than a message that disappears after three seconds. Every lodge kiosk
  response is now `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a cached answer cannot survive a
  lock. A hut leader signed in with their own account on their own device is
  unaffected by any of it. Operator detail in the [Lodge Kiosk
  guide](docs/guides/lodge.md#when-a-hut-leader-unlocks-the-kiosk-with-their-pin).
- **The database now prevents contradictory parent and partner records
  (#3292).** The application already refuses to make the same two members both
  direct parent/dependant and partners. A PostgreSQL backstop now applies the
  same rule to concurrent writes and maintenance SQL, for either parent field
  and for pending or confirmed partnerships.

  This migration requires a planned maintenance window. Operators must stop the
  old application and workers, complete the privately approved relationship
  preflight, verify a fresh backup, and obtain a zero-conflict census before
  migrating. The migration fails closed without changing relationship data if
  any overlap remains.
- **Saving an admin settings page no longer fails at random with a bare error
  (#3293).** An administrator who opened a settings page, spent a moment reading
  it and then pressed Save could get a blunt failure - on Lodge Maintenance it
  read simply "Failed to save" - with nothing written and no explanation. Trying
  again usually worked, which made it look like a glitch in the page.

  Nothing was wrong with the page. The request was never reaching the site at
  all. The web server in front of the application was re-using network
  connections that the application had already closed, and when the two decided
  at the same instant the connection was dropped mid-request. Only actions that
  *save* something could show this: page loads are automatically retried behind
  the scenes, saves cannot be, so a save was the one thing that surfaced it.

  The two timers are now set explicitly, in the right order, so the front-end
  server always lets a connection go before the application does. Fronting this
  application with something other than the bundled Caddy? `DEPLOYMENT.md` →
  "Keep-alive windows must stay ordered" gives the equivalent setting for nginx
  and HAProxy.

  A single dropped connection also used to take the serving instance out of
  rotation for thirty seconds and push live traffic onto the standby, which runs
  a smaller database connection allowance - so one blip became half a minute of
  a slower site. It now takes three failures in a row, so a one-off no longer
  costs anything.
- **The web server now keeps an access log, with credentials stripped out of it
  (#3293).** Until now only *failed* requests were recorded, so there was no way
  to tell how often something went wrong as a share of everything that went
  right - which is exactly the question the fault above raised and nobody could
  answer.

  Ordinary requests are now logged too. Anything that could carry a credential
  is removed before the line is written: the one-time links in emails and on the
  printed lodge QR signs, sign-in codes returned by Google, and payment secrets
  returned by Stripe, in the address, in the referring page's address, and in the
  error log as well as the new access log - the error log had been recording
  these in full. Ordinary web addresses are untouched, so the log is still
  readable.

  Logs go where the rest of the container's output goes and are capped at the
  same size, so nothing needs to be pruned. `DEPLOYMENT.md` → "Access logs" shows
  how to read them.

  **Operators: this release changes `Caddyfile`, so Caddy must be reloaded on the
  host after deploying it** - the app deploy alone does not pick it up. The
  commands are in `DEPLOYMENT.md` → "Public Rate Limits And Proxy Headers".
- **Security: email library patched (#3351).** The Nodemailer library the product sends email through moves to 9.1.1, which closes four published advisories (one rated high) in its address parsing and attachment handling. No change to any message or to how email is sent.
- **A database upgrade that cannot get a lock now stops the deploy cleanly
  instead of freezing the site (#3377).** When a release changes the shape of a
  table, it needs exclusive use of that table for a moment. If something else is
  still using it - a long report, a session somebody left open - the change has
  to wait, and while it waits everything else that wants to read that table
  queues up behind it. Bookings, members and payments are exactly the tables
  involved.

  Until now that wait had no limit, so the only thing that ended it was somebody
  noticing. The deploy notes have been promising a time limit for months; there
  wasn't one. There is now: five seconds, measured rather than guessed. A change
  that cannot get its lock in that time stops, having altered nothing, and the
  deploy halts with the previous release still serving members normally.

  Nothing is left half-finished when this happens, and the upgrade runbook now
  walks an operator through it: find out what was holding the table, clear the
  stopped change, and run the deploy again in a quieter moment. Repeated
  timeouts are deliberately not retried away - they mean something is holding
  onto a busy table during an upgrade, which is worth knowing about.

  Operators who need a different limit can set `MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS`; the
  deploy refuses a value that would switch the protection off or set it so high
  it could never help in time.
- **The six database upgrade steps from the schools-and-membership work were
  renumbered one last time so they run after everything already on the main
  line (#2725, #3391).** Upgrade steps run in the order their names sort, and
  two steps reached the main line while this work was being built - the
  audit-history tidy-up and the member lodge roster - that sort after the
  steps this work adds, even though they were written later. A club upgrading
  to the main line before this work lands would otherwise have had an upgrade
  record whose order disagreed with the step names, for good, and that record is
  what somebody reads when deciding whether an upgrade needs the system taken
  offline. Nothing could have gone wrong - the steps touch different tables and
  none depends on another - and not one step changed; only their names, the
  notes explaining the move, and every place the runbooks name them.
- **A school's booking draws as a whole-lodge blockout on the lodge display
  again, however small the group (#3369, #3391).** Since the schools work
  moved school bookings off their stand-in member records, the lobby display
  was asking "is this a school?" in a way that only the old records could
  answer yes to, so a school party under the eight-person group threshold with
  the lodge to itself appeared as an ordinary booking row rather than a
  blockout. Names were never affected - the school was still labelled by its
  name and its students were never shown. The display now asks the question
  the same way the member lodge roster does, and both surfaces carry a test
  for a school booking in its new shape.
- **The parent/partner exclusivity upgrade now follows every migration already
  queued for release (#3409).** Its deployment-safe backstop is unchanged, but
  operators must use the new `20260929010000` migration path in the documented
  maintenance-window sequence.
- **The audit log now says who changed the club's Xero connection, and who
  turned on a member's two-factor sign-in (#3454).** Connecting Xero,
  disconnecting it, and every automatic token refresh are now recorded:
  connecting and disconnecting name the administrator who did it, and a refresh
  names the background job. Before, the trail recorded nothing at all about the
  tokens. Saving a new Xero client id or secret still disconnects Xero, but the
  save and the disconnect now happen together as one action. They can no longer
  be split by a failure, and the log entry for the disconnect names the
  credential that caused it. The Xero tokens are now held in the same encrypted
  store as the club's other provider credentials. Turning on two-factor sign-in
  is recorded too, as are replacing the recovery codes and clearing it all when
  an account is erased. The member can see their own enrolment on their
  activity history. These entries
  are filed under Security, so anyone who can read Security entries in the
  audit log (including a support-only operator) can see them. That audience is
  one entry type wider than before, and deliberately so: they hold no secret,
  only what changed (two-factor turned on, recovery codes replaced, or the
  second factor cleared) and by which method.
  Nothing changes for the operator: the existing connection keeps working
  through the upgrade without a reconnect.
- **A database upgrade step for the schools work was renumbered so it runs after
  the audit-history tidy-up rather than before it (#2725).** Upgrade steps run in
  the order their names sort, and one that reached the main line while this piece
  of work was being built happened to sort after the schools step even though it
  was written later. Nothing could have gone wrong - the two touch completely
  different tables and neither depends on the other - but a club's upgrade record
  would have shown steps applied in an order that disagreed with their names, for
  good, and that is the record somebody reads when deciding whether an upgrade
  needs the system taken offline. The step itself is unchanged; only its name and
  the note explaining the move.
- **The production deploy script now refuses to ship a release nobody else has,
  keeps the previous release recoverable, and leaves a written record when it
  fails part-way (#3539).** Four changes to
  `scripts/run-production-blue-green-deploy.sh`, each one prompted by something
  that really happened on a live deployment rather than by tidiness. They only
  affect clubs that self-host with the blue/green deploy script; nothing changes
  for anyone using the site.

  **A commit that exists on no remote is refused.** Production once ran code
  built by hand on the deploy host from a branch that was never pushed. It could
  not be rebuilt, could not be reviewed, and silently invalidated the next
  release's preparation - the list of pending database changes, the safety
  ledger and the upgrade notes are all worked out against the commit the
  repository has, not the one running. The deploy now checks before it starts
  and stops if the commit is nowhere but that disk. Building from a local branch
  is still allowed during a registry outage; it just has to be a decision
  somebody wrote down, so it takes both a switch and a written reason and the
  reason goes into the deploy log.

  **The previous release can still be rolled back to.** Rolling back means
  pointing the web server at the colour that was serving before, and that needs
  its images still on the host - but the deploy's own disk cleanup was deleting
  them. It removes the old colour's container near the end, which leaves the old
  image used by nothing, and then prunes it. The deploy reported success while
  the rollback it documents had quietly become impossible. The deploy now pins
  those images before it cleans anything, and pins them by image identity rather
  than by name, because in a locally-built deploy the *name* is moved onto the
  new image half way through.

  **A deploy that dies after changing the database leaves a record.** From that
  point the database may match neither the old release nor the new one, and the
  only account of what happened was whatever was still on the operator's screen.
  Any failure from that step onward now writes a file - into
  `$HOME/tacbookings-deploy-failures` unless you point
  `DEPLOY_FAILURE_RECORD_DIR` somewhere else - naming the step it died on, the
  release attempted, whether traffic had moved, and - most importantly - which
  database changes had *started*, including any that began and did not
  finish. If the database could not be reached at all, the record says that,
  rather than reporting "nothing happened" in the one situation where that would
  be the most misleading thing it could say.

  **Images built on the host now carry the release identifier.** Building by
  hand skipped the details the automated build supplies, so the resulting image
  could not say which release it was. That left the pre-cutover page-warming
  check unable to confirm it had warmed the right release, and the public
  website's security header falling back to a per-build value. There is now a
  supported `--build-and-push-images` mode that passes the same details, and it
  starts the image it just built and reads the identifier back out before
  pushing anything. It also fixes a latent fault on the same path, where the
  build step tried to read the commit from a copy of the code that deliberately
  has no version history, and the deploy aborted with no explanation.
- **Every booking made before the booking ledger existed can now be given its
  ledger lines, so the ledger can be proved against the club's whole history
  (#3583).** `pnpm run booking-ledger:back-post` records each past booking's
  price, payments, account credit, refunds, change fees, edits and
  cancellation in the ledger, using the same rules that record a new booking
  today. It shows what it would record before it records anything, records
  each booking on its own, and records nothing new when run a second time.
  It checks every booking against the ledger census as it goes. Where a
  booking's figures would not agree, it records nothing for that booking and
  lists it with the reason and both figures for an officer to look at. It
  never estimates a figure, never changes an existing entry, and contacts no
  payment or accounting provider. The ledger is still not used for anything a
  member or officer sees; the owner's step-by-step run is in the maintenance
  guide, and the same sequence now runs on every change against a test
  history.
- **Switching off a member's login now ends their access straight away
  (#3603).** Turning off "Can log in" for a member, including handing a family
  group's login to another member, now signs that person out on their next
  request. Until now, someone who was already signed in could keep carrying out
  admin actions, and keep using the finance area and the lodge kiosk, until
  their session ran out. Admin pages themselves were already closed to them.

  Every check that decides what a signed-in person may do now takes the login
  switch into account: admin actions, the finance area, the lodge kiosk and its
  preview, member pages, and help-assistant answers. The time of the switch-off
  is recorded against the member, so signing out is final: if login is switched
  back on, the member signs in again as normal, and any session from before the
  switch-off stays ended.

  Hut-leader PINs are not affected. A PIN belongs to a hut-leader assignment
  and keeps working while the member is active, because hut leaders can be
  members who have never had a login.

  This release includes two small database migrations. The first adds the
  switch-off time; the second records it for every member whose login is
  already off, so their earlier sessions are covered too. Nothing else changes about who holds which
  role: a member whose login is off keeps their stored roles, so the existing
  protections still apply, and such an account still cannot be merged away or
  deleted while it holds Full Admin.
- **The app uses patched Next.js and Axios releases (#3755).** The framework
  and Xero HTTP client's dependency versions now include fixes for reported
  critical and high severity advisories.
- **The remaining URI-parser dependency advisory is fixed (#3783).** The
  app's Prisma and build dependency graphs now use the patched fast-uri 3.1.8.
- The old Xero token table is gone. Tokens stay in the credential store.
  Deploying this release needs the maintenance window in
  [UPGRADING.md](docs/UPGRADING.md). A mistake while the previous release is
  still refreshing leaves Xero on a dead token, and the fix is an administrator
  reconnect.
- **`NODE_BUILD_OPTIONS` now reaches the migration image build too (#3824).**
  Setting `NODE_BUILD_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096` in `.env` (added in
  #2977) fixed an out-of-memory `docker compose build` for the app image, but
  the migration image builds the same stage and never received it. On a machine
  that needed the setting, the app built and then `docker compose run --rm
  migrate` failed with the same "JavaScript heap out of memory" error.

  One setting now covers both builds. Nothing changes for a deployment that
  does not set it.
- **The cut-over ledger check now understands a review completed after a paid
  booking was cancelled (#3907).** Since #3835, a review completed after a
  cancellation on a booking paid by card or internet banking gives back only
  what is still owed, partly to the card or by bank transfer and partly as
  account credit. The ledger check (`pnpm run booking-ledger:census`) only knew
  the credit part, so it reported every such booking as unexplained and held
  the cut-over, even though the money was right.

  It now checks each of those reviews against the refund that review itself
  made - the card refund it queued, or the bank transfer it recorded - together
  with the credit it gave back. A review whose figures do not add up to the
  cent is still reported, and still holds the cut-over. Nothing about what a
  member is refunded has changed.

  Where the credit given back on one cancelled booking could be shared
  between its reviews in more than one way, nothing records which review
  each part belongs to, so lines swapped between them would still add up.
  The check now reports such a booking for the owner to check by hand and
  sign off to the cent, as it already did for a booking that is not
  cancelled, rather than passing it. A booking with so many reviews and
  credits that this cannot be worked out quickly is reported the same way,
  so the check never stalls on it.
- **Two August data backfills now have safety ledger entries, and one of them
  needs a maintenance window (#3933).** The deploy safety ledger had no entry
  for `20260810010000_backfill_booking_request_guest_nights` (#2739) or
  `20260810020000_backfill_bed_allocation_audit_category` (#2751), so an
  operator looking them up before a deploy found no answer.

  If your deployment has **not yet applied** `20260810010000`, the next upgrade
  must now use the windowed deploy sequence: build and validate the new images,
  remove traffic, stop the old app and every old worker, take a fresh verified
  backup, then migrate with the windowed acknowledgements set. The deploy gate
  now asks for them. The reason: while the old version keeps running, a
  requester accepting a booking-request quote leaves the new per-night rows
  carrying the hold's prices instead of the accepted ones, and invoices are
  built from those rows. Requester acceptance cannot be paused in the app, so
  the window is the way to avoid it. The migration ships a `rollback.sql` that
  changes no data on purpose; it holds a read-only query that finds any guest
  whose night prices no longer add up.

  `20260810020000` needs no window, and the post-cutover re-run in the upgrade
  runbook still applies. A deployment that applied both migrations long ago has
  nothing to do, **unless** booking requests were approved between migrate and
  cutover on that deploy. If so, run the query in that `rollback.sql`, and for
  each guest it lists first record the nights' prices with **Record what these
  nights sold for** on the booking's Admin tools card, then refresh the
  booking's invoice.
- **Two fixable dependency security findings are resolved (#3932).** Update source-map-js and smol-toml and re-seal the reviewed braces mitigation inputs without changing its coverage or expiry.
- **Repeating the booking-ledger back-post works again (#3943).** Restore its promotion-delta helper import so repeated runs can correctly report nothing left to post.
- **The sharp image dependency is updated to its security patch (#3962).** Upgrade sharp to 0.35.5 and re-seal the freshly reviewed braces mitigation inputs without changing its coverage, patch or expiry.
- **Maintenance-window deploys check that the old runtime and database clients have stopped (#3963, #4071).** Before applying a pending windowed migration, the production deploy now refuses while any app/web replica is running or another client remains connected to the app database, including idle and external clients. Failed or unknown discovery and drain checks also refuse. Keep the offline window until the new runtime is ready: these checks are snapshots and do not disconnect clients or prevent them reconnecting.
- **The switch for unnamed adults on school booking requests now actually reaches
  the app (#3964).** The two settings that turn on #3413's pending school-adult
  places, `PENDING_SCHOOL_ADULTS_ENABLED` and
  `BLUE_GREEN_OLD_APP_AND_WORKERS_STOPPED`, were never passed into the app
  containers, so setting them as the upgrade runbook says changed
  nothing and the feature stayed off. `docker-compose.yml` now passes both
  through, empty by default.

  Nothing changes until you set them: empty keeps the feature off, exactly as
  before. Set them only when the runbook's #3413 section says to.
- **Next.js is updated to its 16.3.8 security release (#3995).** Upgrade next and eslint-config-next from 16.3.6 to 16.3.8 for one high, four moderate and one low advisory, and re-seal the braces mitigation inputs on the new lockfile without changing its coverage, patch or expiry.
- **The deploy's checks on a newly started container now retry, and say why
  when they stop (#3965).** On 7 Oct 2026 a deploy stopped at step 15 with
  nothing printed, straight after the new container reported healthy; a check
  by hand moments later passed. Why it stopped is still unknown. This change
  does not fix that cause; it makes the deploy ride out a brief hiccup and,
  if the failure recurs, print what went wrong.

  At steps 14 and 15, before the cutover, the deploy asks the new container
  whether it is ready and which role it is running. Each question
  is now asked again every 2 seconds for up to a minute (set
  `DEPLOY_INTERNAL_READ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` in the deploy shell to change that).
  The same check just after the cutover, at step 17, still asks once, so a
  failure there rolls back as quickly as before.
  Every failed attempt prints a line with the HTTP status; or "no HTTP
  response" with the client error (such as `TimeoutError` or
  `TypeError (ECONNREFUSED)`) when the request got no answer; or, if Docker
  could not reach the container, its exit code and whether the container
  restarted or ran out of memory. When the deploy gives up it prints the last reply and
  whether traffic had already moved. A wrong cron secret or a missing route
  stops the deploy at once instead of waiting.
- **The deploy now catches a second `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE` line written with
  a colon (#4026).** Docker Compose reads `KEY: value` in a `.env` file as well
  as `KEY=value`. The production deploy's check for a duplicated
  `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE` only recognised the `=` form, so a second line such as
  `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE: non-production` further down the file slipped past it,
  and Compose then handed that value to every container.

  The check now counts every shape Compose accepts - indented, `export `-prefixed,
  spaces around the separator, and `=` or `:` - and refuses the deploy at step 3
  when the key appears more than once. A single line in any of those shapes is
  still accepted. The rule lives in one function, `env_assignment_pattern`, in
  `scripts/lib/compose-env-file.sh` (moved there from the deploy script by
  #4980). A fork's own deploy checks can source that library directly, which
  has no side effects, instead of keeping a hand-made copy. Do not source
  `scripts/run-production-blue-green-deploy.sh` to reach it: that starts a
  production deploy.
- **A windowed deploy can no longer switch on school-adult holds by itself
  (#4027).** Since #3964, the settings for the school-booking unnamed-adult
  holds (`PENDING_SCHOOL_ADULTS_ENABLED` and
  `BLUE_GREEN_OLD_APP_AND_WORKERS_STOPPED`) reach the app. But a deploy with a
  maintenance window is run with `BLUE_GREEN_OLD_APP_AND_WORKERS_STOPPED=1` set
  in the operator's shell, and Docker Compose prefers a shell value to `.env`.
  So the new release started with it set. If `.env` already said
  `PENDING_SCHOOL_ADULTS_ENABLED=1`, the holds opened without anyone deciding
  to, and the next ordinary deploy closed them again.

  The production deploy now keeps the shell's
  `BLUE_GREEN_OLD_APP_AND_WORKERS_STOPPED` for its migration check only and
  never passes it to the app. It also refuses, at step 3 of 20, a
  `PENDING_SCHOOL_ADULTS_ENABLED` set in the shell that differs from `.env`,
  and names both values. Editing `.env` and re-running the deploy is now truly
  the only way to change either setting for the app. If you relied on a shell
  export to give the app either value, put it in `.env` instead. When the shell
  has `BLUE_GREEN_OLD_APP_AND_WORKERS_STOPPED=1` and `.env` does not, the deploy
  prints a note at step 3 of 20 saying the shell value is for the migration
  check only.

  The upgrade runbook also gains its missing entry and rollback note for the
  other-lodges database change, `20261112010000_other_lodge_beds_and_facilities`,
  which needs a maintenance window.
- **Two-factor sign-in loads the signed-in page fully (#4060).** Accepted codes now open the resolved destination with a fresh page load, addressing the blank destination observed in isolated browser tests. Enrollment still keeps recovery codes on screen until the member presses **Continue**.
- **The booking-ledger census now explains a refund appeal paid back after a
  cancellation (#4120).** An approved refund appeal gives the member back more
  than the cancellation kept, and no charge line on the ledger says so. So once
  any appeal was paid back, by card or by bank transfer, the census reported
  the cancelled booking as an unexplained difference. It now names it
  `REFUND_APPEAL_PAID`, sized from what each approved appeal has actually
  refunded: the same figure the refund-requests screen shows as "Refunded". An
  appeal not yet paid, dismissed or declined explains nothing, and nor does one
  paid for a different amount than the ledger shows, so those still read as
  differences. An appeal's own bank-transfer task, and its card refund while
  Stripe retries it, are also no longer counted as the cancellation's own
  refund in flight or kept. Because the census now agrees, the ledger
  back-post can post such a booking's history instead of refusing it. As the
  owner decided on #4075, an appeal paid back exactly as recorded is listed
  only and needs no sign-off before the ledger switch-over. The census reads
  only; no money or Xero note changes.

  Also: an appeal refunded to the group organiser's card now counts only once
  that refund is actually made, on the refund-requests screen as in the census.
  And an appeal's card refund closed as "paid another way" for less than was
  owed now counts only the part paid back: the screen says how much "was
  closed without being paid back", and the census agrees with the ledger.
- **The booking-ledger check now reads a booking cancelled because the dates
  filled up while the member was paying (#4147).** That cancellation refunds
  the card under its own refund record, which the check did not look at, so
  it could not explain the booking's money. A refund still being retried read
  as wrong, a refund that could not be planned in full could not be accounted
  for, and a refund whose retries had stopped was wrongly treated as
  explained. The check now reads that refund record by the same rule the
  booking page uses. A refund still being retried is shown as in progress.
  Any part of the charge the payment's records captured that the automatic
  refund did not cover is named as planned short, marked as a capacity race,
  for the officers to follow up; a charge the records never captured is
  reported as a separate gap in those records. A refund that can no longer
  be made is still reported as a disagreement. It also means the one-off
  job that writes old bookings into the ledger no longer refuses such a
  booking while its refund is still being retried.
- **Security updates for two third-party packages (#4266).** `follow-redirects`
  (used by the Xero client) moves to 1.16.1, and the test tooling's `vite` to
  8.3.4, closing two newly published high-severity advisories. No behaviour
  change for a club.
- **Caddy can now sit behind a proxy that terminates TLS (#4275).** The
  shipped Caddy configuration assumed Caddy was the public edge and always
  fetched its own certificates from Let's Encrypt. An installation with Nginx
  Proxy Manager or a similar proxy in front could never complete that
  validation, so a freshly created Caddy container had no certificate, the
  proxy answered "502 Bad Gateway", and the deploy's final outside health check
  failed and rolled the cutover back.

  A new `.env` setting, `CADDY_TLS_MODE`, selects how Caddy obtains
  certificates: `acme` (the default, unchanged) or `local`, where Caddy issues
  its own from its internal CA and the proxy is told to accept them. The deploy
  preflight refuses any other value, and checks the Caddy configuration with
  the mode and settings Caddy will actually run with, before the database
  migration rather than at the cutover. The deployment guide has a new section,
  "Behind a TLS-terminating proxy", with the proxy settings to match and the
  safe way to apply a change (re-run the deploy; running Compose from the
  checkout can point the site at the wrong container).

  Behind that proxy, the only address Caddy sees is the proxy's, so the
  per-visitor rate limits on signing in and the audit log's IP column would
  all have become the proxy. In `local` mode Caddy now takes the visitor's
  address from the proxy, and forwarded-address trust is strict and explicit:
  `CADDY_TRUSTED_PROXIES` must name the proxy's own address (the deploy refuses
  local mode without it), and Caddy believes only the address that proxy
  added. Nothing changes in `acme` mode.
- **The production deploy no longer demands AWS SES keys from a club that
  sends mail through its own SMTP relay (#4275).** The deploy script's step-3
  preflight required `AWS_SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and
  `SES_SNS_TOPIC_ARN` whatever the `.env` said about the mail provider, so an
  installation with `USE_SMTP_RELAY=true` and those keys legitimately blank,
  exactly as the configuration guide describes, was refused with "Missing
  required .env entry" before anything was deployed.

  The preflight now follows the provider flags the way the application does,
  and reads them as the application will receive them, after Docker Compose's
  defaults and any value exported in the shell: SES keys for AWS SES, the four
  `EMAIL_SERVER_*` keys for an SMTP relay or a capture mailbox. Because
  Compose defaults `USE_AWS_SES` to `true`, a relay needs `USE_AWS_SES=false`
  as well as `USE_SMTP_RELAY=true`, and the refusal says so. It refuses the
  states the application refuses (two flags true, none true, a value other
  than true or false) and a capture mailbox on the live site, all at step 3
  rather than at the health check. Nothing changes for a club running AWS SES.

  The same preflight also demanded `LEGACY_DASHBOARD_EXPORT_TOKEN`, which the
  configuration guide says to leave empty unless the legacy finance export
  bridge is still in use. It is now optional: blank passes and disables the
  bridge, while a placeholder value is still refused.

  A fork's image names (`GHCR_APP_IMAGE_REPOSITORY` and
  `GHCR_MIGRATE_IMAGE_REPOSITORY`) are now also read from the source
  repository's `.env` when the shell does not set them, with the same rules
  Compose applies to that file (quotes, `export`, the last duplicate wins),
  instead of falling straight back to the upstream registry, and step 3/8
  says which source each name came from. A deploy run under `sudo`, which
  strips the shell environment, therefore still pulls the fork's own images.
- **The database connection ceiling can be raised from `.env` (#4275).** A
  routine blue/green handover on a live host was measured at 39 open client
  connections, with one app container holding 18 against
  a configured limit of 10, so the deploy's pre-cutover warm-up found every
  public page failing with "too many database connections opened" and refused
  to switch, even though the previous release kept serving.

  `POSTGRES_MAX_CONNECTIONS` in `.env` now sets Postgres's `max_connections`
  for the compose database service. The default stays at 40, so nothing
  changes for an installation that does not set it; a host that sees that
  error raises it, for example to 80, and the next deploy recreates the
  database container with the new ceiling. The deploy refuses a value that is
  not a whole number above the connection pools the configuration can open
  together, or that is above 1000, before it touches the database container.
  The deployment guide's "Connection pool sizing" section records the
  measurement and why raising the ceiling, not shrinking a pool, is the right
  response.

  `POSTGRES_MEM_LIMIT` (default `768m`, unchanged) lets a host raise the
  database container's memory in step with the ceiling. The cause of the
  measurement, one app container holding more connections than its pool
  allows, was fixed at its source in #4269.
- **Deeply nested HTML no longer breaks sanitization (#4281).** Upgrade
  sanitize-html to 2.18.1 to bound discarded iframe fallbacks and preserve the
  nesting limit. The existing braces patch, scope and expiry stay unchanged.
- **Next.js 16.4.1 and DOMPurify 3.4.17 close six dependency advisories (#4309).**
  GitHub published advisories on 23 October 2026 against the Next.js release
  the site ran on (two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution, and one
  denial of service) and against the DOMPurify copy that PDF export pulls in.
  Both move to their patched releases; nothing in the app's own code changes.
  The braces mitigation record (#3843) is refreshed on unchanged evidence with
  the new lockfile digest and a new expiry. Deployments pick the fix up with
  the next image build.
- **Four dependency advisories published on 24 October 2026 are closed (#4326).**
  `zod` moves to 4.6.7, `nodemailer` (the mail sender) to 10.2.1, and the
  test-tooling copies of `undici` (8.12.3) and `fast-uri` (3.1.9) to their
  patched releases. Nothing in the app's own code changes. The required
  dependency audit is clean again, and no mitigation record is needed.
- **One database pool per container, not one per server bundle (#4269).**
  Next builds the application's database client into several server bundles, and
  each one opened its own connection pool: a container set to 10 connections was
  measured holding 22 under load, which is what ran Postgres out of connections
  during a blue/green handover. The client is now shared across the bundles, and
  the same measurement reads 10. No behaviour changes.
- **Hand-run deployments validate the image Compose actually selects (#4393).** Local image checks now follow Compose's project-name normalization and `.env` settings. An unavailable image reference stops the engine instead of falling back to a guessed tag that could name an older image.
- **A club can now stop the booking system connecting to its database as the
  all-powerful administrator, so the system itself can no longer change the
  booking ledger or the audit log (#4453).** Until now every part of the
  system signed in to the database with the same superuser account, the one
  that can do anything. A fault, or a stolen copy of the system's password,
  could therefore change or delete any record, including the money ledger
  behind every booking and the audit trail of who did what.

  An operator can now split that one account into separate roles. A
  migration role owns the database structure and applies upgrades. The
  application role can add and read ledger lines and audit entries, but cannot
  change them by any route. A small audit-retention role, given only to the
  scheduled-jobs container, does the nightly clean-up of old audit entries and
  nothing else: it can clear an entry's IP address or browser details, but never
  write one. The administrator account is kept for people. A new command,
  `pnpm run db:provision-roles`, sets the roles up. It only shows what it would
  do unless it is run with `--apply`. It stops without changing anything if it
  would have to wait for a busy table, and it checks its own work and undoes
  everything if the result is wrong.

  One thing is deliberately unchanged: **deleting a booking still deletes that
  booking's ledger lines**, as it always has.

  Nothing about the roles changes until a club opts in. The new settings
  (`APP_DB_USER`, `MIGRATION_DB_USER`, their passwords and
  `AUDIT_RETENTION_DATABASE_URL`) are empty by default, and with them empty the
  system connects exactly as before. Switching over and back is an ordinary
  blue/green deploy, and the deploy refuses a half-finished switch.
  `DEPLOYMENT.md` ("Least-privilege database roles") and `docs/UPGRADING.md`
  give the steps.

  Every club gets three smaller changes:
  - The database now refuses any change to a booking's or a lodge's key, which
    a ledger line could be named by. Nothing in the system makes such a change,
    and the release deploys normally.
  - The nightly backup check, which restores each backup into a spare database,
    no longer needs an administrator account. It also now refuses a spare
    database that is really the live one under another name.
  - Once a club switches, restoring a backup over the live database from the
    Backups admin page is refused. An operator restores with the database tools
    instead.

  This replaces the July 2026 decision (#2240) to keep the single administrator
  account.
- **Nightly backups use bounded memory as the database grows (#4487).** Database
  dumps are now compressed to disk as they arrive. Failed or timed-out dumps
  remove their partial file and report failure before copying or uploading it.
  Docker stages compressed files on a disk-backed volume, which keeps a dump only
  while no destination received it and clears anything over an hour old; recreate
  the app and cron containers during the upgrade to apply the new mount.
- Fix the backup restore drill for dumps containing deployment ownership and privilege statements, reusing the restore validator's streaming filter and skipping archive ACLs without modifying the supplied backup (#4483).
- **Deployment images have verifiable build records and pinned inputs (#4455).**
  Actions and external container images now use immutable references, updated
  through Dependabot. Published app and migration images include an SBOM and
  build provenance; the deployment guide explains how to verify them. App
  containers drop Linux capabilities, new npm releases wait seven days before
  installation, and OpenSSF Scorecard reports advisory security findings.
- Keep booking-ledger history when a booking is deleted (#4514, decision D1 on #4482): every key a ledger line holds, a member-credit row's booking links and a group settlement's group key now refuse deletion (RESTRICT), so the database refuses, for every role, to delete a booking that financial history names. Draft deletion leaves such a draft alone (409 on the route; the nightly cleanup reports it), member hard delete refuses a member the journal names as debtor, and the local demo seed refuses a database holding ledger or journal lines. The deploy needs the breaking-migration override; the old colour stays compatible.
- **Payment history survives attempts to delete its parent (#4574).** The database
  refuses to delete payments with transactions and transactions linked to refunds
  or recovery operations. Deploying this protection requires the reviewed
  breaking-migration override described in the upgrade guide.
- **Maintenance scripts now run when started through a linked folder
  (#4598).** About forty of the repository's command-line scripts decided
  whether they had been run directly by comparing two spellings of their own
  path. Started from a checkout reached through a symbolic link, some of them
  quietly did nothing and still reported success.

  Every script now asks one shared helper, which compares the real location of
  both paths, and a test fails any script that writes its own check again.
  Nothing changes for an operator running the scripts the usual way.
- A signed-in session now records when the person last proved who they are. They can confirm again with an authenticator code, or with their password if they have no app and no passkey, and an emailed code is never accepted. Nothing asks for that confirmation yet.
- **Members can use a passkey as the second sign-in step (#4617).**
  On Profile, under Security, a member can add a passkey and remove one they
  no longer want. Adding or removing a passkey does not turn the authenticator
  app or email code on or off.

  The next sign-in is still the password, then the passkey when one is saved,
  shown beside the app or email code and the recovery code. Confirm-it's-you
  can use that same passkey. An emailed code still cannot confirm a session.
  The passkey is bound to this site's address (`NEXTAUTH_URL`).
- Officers who can move money or change system settings, and every Full Admin, can be required to use an authenticator app or a passkey, with a grace period and a way back from a lost device. The requirement stays off until a later change turns it on, so a club that updates now is asked of the same people as today.
- Saving the officer two-factor policy writes one new security audit row, which anyone with Support view can read, like the password-policy save. The policy is not carried by configuration export or import.
- **Officers see no change when they restore a backup, refund a payment,
  export members, or change credentials and roles (#4619).** Those actions
  now check for a fresh confirmation. The check is switched off, so the
  dialog does not appear until a later release turns it on. Nothing new to
  configure.
- **Repeated wrong passwords on one account are now slowed down, however many
  internet addresses they come from (#4609).** Until now the only brake on
  password guessing was per internet address, so someone guessing an officer's
  password from many addresses at once was never slowed. Now, after five
  unsuccessful password attempts on one account, each further attempt on that
  account waits: 30 seconds, then doubling up to 15 minutes. An hour with no
  attempt forgets the count, and a correct password after the wait signs in as
  usual and clears it - so does a completed password reset.

  The wait looks exactly the same whether or not the account exists, so it
  cannot be used to find out who has an account, and no email address is
  stored: the count is kept against a scrambled key. Emailed sign-in links,
  Google sign-in and the two-factor step are unaffected, and the sign-in page
  points members at them when the club has them switched on. Members signing in
  normally see no change. One limit to know: someone who keeps guessing can keep
  an account's password sign-in waiting, so a club whose officers rely on
  password sign-in alone may want emailed sign-in links switched on.
- **Sign-in checks use the same password hashing cost for unknown accounts and new passwords (#4639).** This closes a timing difference that could reveal an account exists. Existing passwords keep their original hashing cost until replaced.
- **Repeated current-password guesses now trigger a wait (#4640).** Changing a password shares sign-in's per-account attempt limit. A member must wait before trying again after repeated failures, and a valid current password clears the shared count.
- **A new password that has already leaked in a public data breach is now
  refused (#4610).** Until now a password only had to meet the club's length
  and character rules, so a password reused from a breached website was
  accepted, and those are the passwords attackers try first.

  When someone changes their password, chooses one from a reset or
  account-setup link, or an officer sets a kiosk password, the app now checks it
  against a public list of breached passwords and asks for a different one if
  it is listed. The password never leaves the server: only the first five
  characters of a one-way code made from it are sent, and the comparison is
  made by the app. Passwords already set are not re-checked, and sign-in is
  unchanged.

  The check is on by default. A club can switch it off under **Admin → Login &
  Security → Password policy**. If the breach list does not answer within three
  seconds the password is accepted, so an outage never stops anyone setting a
  password. A server that restricts outbound traffic must allow HTTPS to
  `api.pwnedpasswords.com` for the check to work (`CONFIGURATION.md`).
- **The lodge kiosk tablet now really stays signed in for 30 days without use
  (#4612).** The kiosk account was meant to stay signed in on the shared lodge
  tablet for 30 days, but the setting never took effect: like every other
  account, it was signed out after 8 hours without use, so a quiet night could
  leave the tablet needing someone with the kiosk password.

  The kiosk account now stays signed in for 30 days without use, and each time
  the kiosk page is opened or brought back to the front the 30 days start again.
  Only the kiosk account itself gets this: the account whose User Type is
  "Lodge (kiosk account)", which has no role besides User and Lodge. Every
  other account still signs out after 8 hours without use, including an admin
  or officer who also has the Lodge box ticked, and anyone who signs in with
  their own account on the kiosk tablet. A person's record with only User and
  Lodge ticked counts as the kiosk too, so give that person a second role or
  untick Lodge. Give the kiosk account itself a second role and its next refresh
  drops it to 8 hours. A hut leader's PIN unlock is unchanged: it still locks
  after 10 minutes without use.
- **Changing the lodge kiosk password now signs out the tablet.** Saving a new kiosk password under **Admin → Lodge Operations → Lodge Kiosk** used to leave a tablet already signed in under the old password signed in, for up to 30 days. It is now signed out the next time it refreshes, so rotating the password after a lost tablet or a departure takes effect; sign the tablet in again with the new password.
- **Password-reset and sign-in-link emails are now limited per member, not
  just per internet address (#4613).** Someone sending requests from many
  addresses could previously make the club send one member a stream of
  "forgot password" or "sign-in link" emails they never asked for, at the cost
  of the club's sending quota and email reputation.

  Each of those emails now goes to one account at most 3 times an hour,
  however many addresses ask. A request past that limit gets the usual "check
  your email" answer and sends nothing, exactly as for an email address the
  club does not know, so the limit reveals nothing about who is a member. If a
  member says a reset or sign-in email never arrived, ask them to wait an hour
  and try again. No email address is stored for this count, and nothing needs
  setting up.
- **Every sign-in now ends after a fixed time, however busy it is (#4611).**
  Until now a session ended only after 8 hours without use, and every page load
  pushed that forward, so a browser in daily use, or a stolen session cookie,
  could stay signed in for ever.

  Each sign-in now also lasts at most a set time, counted from when the person
  signed in. Nothing extends it: not using the site, not a role change, not a
  two-factor check. When the time is up the next page sends the person to sign
  in again. The default is 7 days; a club can choose any whole number of hours
  from 8 to 720 (30 days) under **Admin → Login & Security → Password policy**
  ("Sign members out after (hours)"), and a change applies to people already
  signed in. The lodge kiosk account keeps its own 30 days, which the club
  setting does not change, so the lodge tablet must be signed in again once a
  month.

  On upgrade, anyone who signed in more than 7 days earlier (30 days for the
  lodge tablet) is asked to sign in again on their next page load.
- **Stored credentials and two-factor secrets can now be protected by their own
  key instead of the sign-in secret (#4456).** Until now `AUTH_SECRET`, which
  signs every session, was also the key every stored provider credential (Xero,
  Stripe, Google, backups, the AI and Alpine Central Server keys) and every
  member's authenticator-app secret was encrypted under. A leak of that one
  value exposed all of it, and changing it after a leak destroyed it.

  A new, optional setting, `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`, holds a separate key (or a
  list of them, the first used for new data). Once it is set, new and re-saved
  credentials, authenticator enrolments and Xero token refreshes are encrypted
  under it, and the auth secret can later be rotated without losing them.
  The site runs unchanged until an operator sets it, but Admin → Setup has a
  new "Data Encryption Key" step saying what is still on the auth secret, and
  on a club with a stored provider credential or authenticator-app secret that
  step is red, so the setup report shows blocked and `pnpm run setup:check`
  exits 1 until a key is set.

  **What to do:** read "Data-encryption keys" in `CONFIGURATION.md` and "Adding
  a data-encryption key" in `DEPLOYMENT.md`. Set the key only after every
  container runs this release. **Recovery codes issued before the key is set
  stop working when it is set**; affected members see a notice at sign-in and
  on their profile asking them to generate new ones, and admins should
  regenerate their own straight away. Until a later release deletes them, the
  old codes work again on any server without the key. Add a newer key later in
  two redeploys, as `DEPLOYMENT.md` describes.
- **Moving stored secrets onto the data-encryption key, and switching the old
  key off (#4456).** A new command, `pnpm run data-keys:reencrypt`, moves every
  stored provider credential and authenticator-app secret that is still under
  `AUTH_SECRET`, or under an older data key, onto the current
  `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` key. Values and members' authenticator apps are
  unchanged. It is safe to run while the site serves traffic: a row that
  changes while it is being moved, such as a Xero token refresh, wins and is
  retried. `--dry-run` only counts. A run that writes needs
  `--expect-fingerprint`, copied from Admin → Setup → "Data Encryption Key",
  and refuses unless its own key matches, so a stale `.env` cannot move data
  under the wrong key. The report ends with what remains on old keys and never
  prints a key or a stored value. The setup step stays amber while a
  credential or an authenticator-app secret is under an older key in the ring;
  unused recovery codes under it are only listed, since removing that key
  retires them. Each move is recorded in the
  audit log under the `data-key-reencrypt` job.

  With `--retire-legacy-recovery-codes` it also retires the recovery codes
  issued before the key was set, so they stop working on every server, with or
  without the key. Members holding them keep seeing the notice asking them to
  generate a new set.

  A new optional setting, `DATA_ENCRYPTION_LEGACY_KEY=retired`, stops the site
  reading anything under `AUTH_SECRET` once the command reports nothing left on
  it. After that, the auth secret signs sessions and links and protects no
  stored data. Unset it to undo.

  **What to do:** nothing until you have set `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`. Then
  follow "Moving stored data to the current key" and "Retiring the legacy key"
  in `DEPLOYMENT.md`. Run the command only once every container has the key.
- **New installs set up restricted database roles and a separate encryption key before first use (#4904).** First Bootstrap now walks the operator through both steps. Setup warns when its database connection has superuser rights, and the setup wizard reminds the operator when the data key is missing. Existing installations keep working with their current settings.
- **Keep sign-out available on busy shared networks (#4917).** Sign-out and session updates no longer use the sign-in address budget. Sign-in allows 30 attempts per 15 minutes per address, alongside the existing per-account password throttle. Refused sign-ins show a network wait message, and an unused emailed sign-in link can be retried.
- **A new live site can no longer start up believing it is a test copy
  (#4980).** The first-install steps in `DEPLOYMENT.md` copy `.env.example`,
  which declares `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE=non-production`. A live site started from
  it unchanged held back every member email and replaced the email addresses on
  the club's real Xero contacts, while **Admin → Setup** showed a green tick.

  First Bootstrap now tells you to set `APP_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE=production` and to
  run `bash scripts/check-environment-role.sh` before the first
  `docker compose up`. The check refuses anything but exactly `production`,
  names the setting, and starts nothing. It is the same check the production
  deploy already runs at step 3, now shared by both.

  On **Admin → Setup**, the **Production Or Non-Production** step now shows an
  amber warning when the deployment declares non-production: "If this is the
  club's live site, members are getting no email and Xero contact addresses are
  being replaced." On a real copy (staging, a restore rehearsal, a laptop),
  press **Acknowledge** once. A copy forced by the safer override inside the app
  stays green. Expect staging to show the warning until someone acknowledges it.
- **The legacy finance dashboard route and the extra hostnames are now settings,
  off unless a club asks for them (#4981).** Every installation used to serve
  the original club's `/finance-legacy` route (forwarded to a fixed private
  address), plus `bookings.`, `dashboard.` and `www.` versions of its domain.
  A club without those DNS records saw certificate errors for hostnames it
  never created, and could not remove them without blocking its next deploy.

  `CADDY_LEGACY_ROUTES` (default `off`) now turns the legacy route and the
  `bookings.`/`dashboard.` hosts on, with the dashboard's address in
  `CADDY_FINANCE_LEGACY_UPSTREAM`. `CADDY_WWW_REDIRECT` (default `on`) can turn
  the `www.` redirect off. The deploy refuses a mistyped value, or the legacy
  route without an address, before it changes anything.

  **Action needed only if your club used `/finance-legacy` or the `bookings.`
  or `dashboard.` hostnames:** set `CADDY_LEGACY_ROUTES=on` and
  `CADDY_FINANCE_LEGACY_UPSTREAM` in `.env` before deploying this release.
  `DEPLOYMENT.md` → "Hostnames and DNS records" lists the DNS record each
  hostname needs.
- **An emailed link, Google, or a recovery code no longer counts as confirming
  who you are (#4994).** The five-minute confirmation clock now starts for a
  password only when no authenticator app is still owed, and for an
  authenticator-app code. An emailed second factor does not count as still
  owed, so that password starts the clock and the later emailed code leaves
  it where it is. Signing in from an emailed link or with Google, or finishing
  with a recovery code, leaves the clock unset, so the first protected action
  asks for a password. Nothing asks for that confirmation yet.
- **Two-factor set-up shows a QR code, and Enter submits the code (#4952).**
  Setting up an authenticator app now shows a QR code to scan, drawn in the
  browser so the secret never leaves the page, with the setup key still shown
  underneath for typing. The App, Email and Recovery choices on the set-up and
  sign-in screens now say which one is selected, in words and to screen
  readers, rather than by shading alone. Pressing Enter in a code box enrols or
  verifies, as clicking the button does.
- **Deploy helpers and security scans now use fixed container builds (#4906).**
  The deploy's temporary Caddy containers use the same pinned image as Compose.
  Security scans, CI databases and the backup drill also use digest pins, with
  a check that rejects floating third-party images before they reach CI.
- **System Health and the health checks now show the release that is actually
  installed (#4985).** Every release used to report version "0.1.0" on
  **Admin → Monitoring & Support → System Health**, `/api/health` and
  `/api/health/ready`, and to file server-side Sentry errors under release
  "0.1.0". Config-transfer exports and the diagnostics support-evidence pack
  recorded the version as "unknown".

  The version is now taken from the release itself when the app is built, so all
  of these show the real version (for example 0.13.2) with no setting to add.
  Browser and edge Sentry events are not changed by this release.
  If an uptime monitor reads the `version` field from a health check, expect it
  to change from "0.1.0" to the real version after this upgrade.
- **Servers that build the image themselves should set
  `NODE_BUILD_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192` (#5164).** The production
  build's type check now needs about 4.6 GB of Node heap, more than Node's
  default ceiling and more than the `4096` the docs used to suggest, so a build
  could stop with "JavaScript heap out of memory" or "Failed to type check".

  CI's builds now run with an 8 GB ceiling, and `.env.example`,
  `CONFIGURATION.md` and the upgrade notes recommend the same value. It affects
  the build only, never the running app. A server that deploys a published
  image builds nothing and needs no change.
- **The production deploy now refuses a commit that is not a published release, and the install steps start from a release (#4978).** `scripts/run-production-blue-green-deploy.sh`, in both its deploy and its `--build-and-push-images` mode, now checks with `origin` that an annotated release tag such as `v0.13.2` points at the commit it is about to deploy. If none does, it stops before any image, workspace or migration is touched. A lightweight tag, a tag that only exists on the deploy host, and an `origin` that cannot be reached are all refused too.

  **What operators need to do.** Until the next release is cut, plain `main` is not a release, so every production deploy of `main` needs the override: set `ALLOW_UNTAGGED_DEPLOY_COMMIT=1` and a written `UNTAGGED_DEPLOY_COMMIT_REASON` in the shell (not `.env`, and pass them through if you use `sudo`). The reason is printed in the deploy log. Staging hosts that deploy `main` on purpose need the same two variables. To deploy a release instead, run `git fetch origin tag <tag>` and then `DEPLOY_REF=<tag> ./scripts/run-production-blue-green-deploy.sh`. A fork that does not tag its own releases either tags them with `pnpm run release:cut` or sets the override on every deploy.

  The install steps in the Implementation Guide and in "First Bootstrap" in `DEPLOYMENT.md` now check out the latest release tag straight after `git clone`, so a new club no longer installs whatever `main` held that day. The three `v0.10.0` draft files moved to `docs/releases/drafts/`, so `docs/releases/` lists only published releases.
- **Rebuilding the app image is faster after the first build.** The Docker
  build now keeps Next.js's build cache between builds on the same machine, so
  an operator rebuilding after `git pull` no longer compiles the whole app from
  nothing. The image itself is unchanged: the cache never goes into it.

  For contributors, the browser test run in CI also finishes sooner: its shards
  are balanced by how long each test file takes, they no longer wait for the
  build cache to upload, and videos are recorded only for retried tests.
- A Docker-only install can now create its first admin. `docker compose run --rm seed` runs the base seed in a one-shot service on the migrate image, and `DEPLOYMENT.md` "First Bootstrap" gives it as step 7, once the database roles are on; the command three docs gave, which ran the seed with `exec` in the app container, failed because the app image holds no source.
